title: First-nun roots

objectives.can: Recognise forms where a first נ has assimilated or dropped, and restore the root.

explanation.summary: A נ at the end of a syllable, before another consonant, is not pronounced separately: it is absorbed by the next consonant, which is written doubled. That one habit explains why the verbs for 'fall', 'give', 'lift' and 'strike' lose a consonant in the yiqtol, the wayyiqtol, the Niphal and the Hiphil, and why some of their imperatives and infinitives are so short. The aim is to read a doubled consonant and know that a נ is missing in front of it.

sections.heading: The cause: a nun that closes a syllable
body: In a root whose first consonant is נ, the נ is the first sound after a prefix whenever the verb takes one: in the yiqtol and wayyiqtol (after the prefix of person), in the Hiphil qatal (after the prefix הִ), in the Hiphil yiqtol (after יַ), and in the Niphal. In all of those the נ would close a syllable and be followed at once by the next root consonant with no vowel between them. Hebrew does not keep this cluster. The נ assimilates: it takes on the sound of the next consonant, which is therefore written with a doubling dagesh.

Compare the qatal and the participle of the same verb. In נָפַל and נֹפֵל the נ is followed by a vowel, so it is a full consonant and nothing is lost. The weakness shows only in the forms where the נ would stand without a vowel.

sections.heading: Qal yiqtol and wayyiqtol
body: Take the verb 'to fall'. Its qatal is נָפַל, with all three consonants visible. Its yiqtol is יִפֹּל and its wayyiqtol וַיִּפֹּל: the prefix is followed directly by a doubled פ, and the נ has gone. A form with a dagesh in the first root consonant is therefore a signal: ask whether the consonant before it could have been a נ. The root of וַיִּתֵּן is not ת-ת-ן; it is נ-ת-ן, 'give', with the נ absorbed into the first ת. The same is true of the root of וַיִּקַּח (the ל of לָקַח behaves exactly like a נ in this respect), of יִשָּׂא from נָשָׂא, and of וַיִּגַּשׁ from נָגַשׁ.

The vowel under the doubled consonant depends on the verb, and the verbs differ: יִפֹּל has ō, יִתֵּן has ē, and וַיִּגַּשׁ and וַיִּקַּח have a. The prefix keeps its ordinary vowel. You need to learn this vowel for each common verb, as you learned it for the regular verbs.

When the third plural ending is added, the נ is still absorbed: וַיִּפְּלוּ. The forms with a first-person prefix show the same pattern: אֶתֵּן, 'I will give', is the yiqtol of נָתַן; אֶשָּׂא is the yiqtol of נָשָׂא. The dagesh in the first root consonant is not always written. In וַיִּסְעוּ, from נָסַע, there is no dagesh to see in the samekh, so the verb must be recognised by the context and the rest of the form; contrast וַיִּסַּע, where the dagesh is present.

sections.heading: The root consonant that is lost altogether
body: In the imperative and the infinitive construct, a נ at the very start of the word is lost entirely in several of the commonest roots. The imperative of נָתַן is תֵּן and תְּנוּ, and of נָשָׂא is שָׂא and שְׂאוּ; the imperative of נָגַשׁ is גַּשׁ, גְּשׁוּ, and of לָקַח it is קַח, קְחוּ. The infinitive construct of נָתַן is תֵּת (and, with the preposition, לָתֵת or לָתֶת); of נָשָׂא it is שְׂאֵת (with the preposition, לָשֵׂאת); of נָגַשׁ it is a form like לָגֶשֶׁת; and of לָקַח it is a form like לָקַחַת. Note the added ת at the end of these infinitives, which gives them the shape of a feminine noun.

This is not a rule for every first-nun root. The imperative of נָטָה keeps its נ (נְטֵה), and so does the imperative of נָפַל (נִפְלוּ); the infinitive construct of נָפַל and נָסַע keeps it as well (בִּנְפֹל, בִּנְסֹעַ). The imperative of נָסַע, וּסְעוּ, has lost its נ, while its infinitive keeps it. So the loss in the imperative and infinitive is a pattern you learn for each verb, not something you can predict from the root class alone.

sections.heading: Niphal and Hiphil
body: The same assimilation appears in the derived stems. The Hiphil qatal of נָגַד is הִגִּיד, with a doubled גּ and no נ; its yiqtol is יַגִּיד, its infinitive construct לְהַגִּיד. The Hiphil of נָצַל is הִצִּיל and יַצִּיל, and of נָכָה it is הִכָּה (a Hiphil qatal, 'he struck'). The Hiphil of נָפַל, וַיַּפֵּל, 'and he made fall', is written in the same way. The participle מַצִּיל and the imperative הַצִּילֵנִי belong to the same family.
The Niphal qatal of נָגַשׁ is נִגַּשׁ: after the Niphal prefix נִ the root's own נ has been absorbed into the doubled גּ, so the form shows only one נ.

sections.heading: Two nuns in one verb: נָתַן
body: The verb 'give' has a נ at both ends. The first assimilates as above. The last one assimilates too, when the ending begins with a consonant and no vowel stands between: נָתַתִּי, 'I gave', and נָתַתָּה, 'you gave', where the ת is the ending's ת joined to the root's final נ. The root has only one ת; the second is the ending. When the ending begins with a vowel, the final נ is a full consonant and stays: נָתְנוּ, נָתְנָה. The unmarked third masculine singular is נָתַן. The participle is נֹתֵן.
A learner who sees נָתַתִּי and looks for a root with ת in the middle will not find נָתַן. Look for a missing final ן, or a missing first נ, before you decide that the root is unfamiliar.

sections.heading: How to restore the root
body: Use three questions. Does the form begin with a prefix of the yiqtol, the wayyiqtol, the Niphal or the Hiphil and have a doubled first root consonant? Then a נ (or ל in the one verb לָקַח) may be missing in front of it. Is it a very short imperative or a short infinitive ending in ת? Then the first consonant may have dropped. Does the form have an ending beginning with ת or נ preceded by a ת or נ? Then the final consonant of the root may have been absorbed. Then compare with a root you know.

misunderstandings: A dagesh in the first root consonant is not always a sign of a first-nun root. A Piel or a Niphal also has a dagesh. Always ask whether the root, with a נ restored in front of the doubled consonant, is a verb you know.

The נ does not always disappear. It is a full consonant in the qatal, the participle and the infinitive absolute, and in some imperatives and infinitives as well. The loss happens where the נ would close a syllable.
לָקַח is not a first-nun verb. Its ל simply behaves like one in the yiqtol, imperative and infinitive. Do not look for a נ at the front of its root.
A doubled ת in נָתַתִּי does not mean that the root has two taws. One ת belongs to the ending.

deeper.heading: Which consonant takes the sound
body: The assimilated נ takes the sound of the consonant that follows it, and this is why you see a doubled consonant of a different shape in each verb: פּ in יִפֹּל, תּ in יִתֵּן, שׂ in יִשָּׂא. The same absorption is found in other Semitic languages, and in Hebrew in a few other roots as well. For reading, it is enough to expect a doubled first consonant after a prefix and to ask which consonant was lost.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat; and she gave also unto her husband with her, and he did eat.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Three wayyiqtols of three roots in a row: וַתִּקַּח (from לָקַח), וַתֹּאכַל (from אָכַל, a first-alef verb) and וַתִּתֵּן (from נָתַן). In the first and the third, the prefix is followed by a doubled consonant, and a נ or ל is missing in front of it: the ק of the first and the ת of the third are doubled. She takes, eats and gives.

examples.analysis: וַיַּפֵּל is a Hiphil wayyiqtol of נָפַל: the Hiphil prefix is followed by a doubled פ, 'and he made fall'. The same verse has וַיִּקַּח from לָקַח, where the ק is doubled: 'and he took'.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And Isaac said unto Jacob: 'Come near, I pray thee, that I may feel thee, my son, whether thou be my very son Esau or not.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: גְּשָׁה is a masculine singular imperative of נָגַשׁ, 'come near'. The initial נ has dropped, and the form starts with the גּ. The added ־ָה lengthens the imperative; it does not change the root.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And Cain said unto the LORD: 'My punishment is greater than I can bear.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: מִנְּשֹׂא is the preposition מִן followed by an infinitive construct of נָשָׂא, 'than bearing'. Here the נ of the root is present, as it is in the infinitives of several first-nun roots when a preposition stands in front: the form is not always the short שְׂאֵת.

quoted.english: And He said: 'Who told thee that thou wast naked? Hast thou eaten of the tree, whereof I commanded thee that thou shouldest not eat?'

examples.analysis: הִגִּיד is the Hiphil qatal, third masculine singular, of נָגַד, 'he told'. The נ has assimilated to the גּ, which is doubled; the stem is recognised by the הִ prefix and the long hireq before the last consonant.
